notes.text: Urdu and Hindi share one grammar. Swap Persian words for Sanskrit ones and speakers cross the line without noticing.
Assalam alaikum comes back reversed as wa alaikum assalam. In Lucknow, adab greets anyone of any faith.
Aap takes a plural verb even for one person: aap kahan rehte hain, never rehta hai. Respect lives in the verb.
English has one word, uncle. Urdu has four: chacha, mamu, khalu, phupha, each naming a different side of the family.
Dastarkhwan is the cloth spread on the floor for a meal. An invitation to yours means far more than dinner.
Even though Urdu runs right to left, numbers still run left to right. Writers change direction mid sentence.
Gulabi, pink, comes from gulab, rose. Persian gul means flower, so the colour is literally named after a bloom.
Safar is a journey, and a hamsafar travels beside you, which is also how people name a life partner.
Kal is yesterday and tomorrow both; parson stretches two days either way. The verb tense settles which direction you mean.
Bazaar reached English from Persian through Urdu. Ask kitne ka hai, how much for it, and expect a counter offer.
When someone falls ill you say Allah shifa de, may God grant healing. A get well wish here is a prayer.
Makan is the building you rent, ghar is the household inside it. Same address, two different words.
Naukri, a salaried job, comes from naukar, servant. Work you own is kaam or karobar, never naukri.
Dil is heart and mind together. Dil chahta hai, the heart wants, is how Urdu says I feel like.
Chand raat, the night the Eid moon is sighted, keeps bangle stalls open till dawn. Then it is Eid Mubarak.
